title: What is the Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) architecture, how does it isolate domain logic from infrastructure (dependency inversion), and why is it a style you layer on top of microservices/monolith rather than an alternative to them?
shortTitle: What is the Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) architecture, how does it isolate domain logic from infrastructure, and why is it a style you layer on top of microservices or a monolith?

s1_definition.profdef: Hexagonal architecture, also called Ports and Adapters, places the domain logic (business rules) at the center and surrounds it with ports — interfaces that define what the domain needs or offers — and adapters — concrete implementations that connect those ports to specific technologies. Inbound adapters (REST controllers, message listeners) drive the application through inbound ports, and the domain reaches the outside world through outbound ports implemented by outbound adapters (database repositories, external API clients). The dependency rule is that everything points inward: the domain depends on nothing, and all infrastructure depends on the domain's interfaces, achieved through dependency inversion. It is a code-organization style that lives inside a single deployable unit, so you apply it within a monolith or within each microservice rather than instead of them.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the loan-approval department at National Bank of India as the heart of the business — the rules for approving a loan never change based on how the application arrived or where records are stored. Around this heart are standardized slots (ports): one slot accepts applications, whether they come by web form, mobile app, or phone. Another slot sends records out, whether to an Oracle database or a flat file. The web form, the mobile app, the Oracle connector, and the file writer are all adapters that plug into these slots. If the bank switches from Oracle to PostgreSQL, you unplug the Oracle adapter and plug in a PostgreSQL adapter — the loan rules in the heart are not touched. The business logic does not know or care what is plugged into its slots.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put the business rules in the center with technology-agnostic ports, plug concrete adapters onto those ports, and make everything depend inward so you can swap any technology without touching the domain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Hexagonal architecture, also called Ports and Adapters, places the domain logic (business rules) at the center and surrounds it with ports — interfaces that define what the domain needs or offers — and adapters — concrete implementations that connect those ports to specific technologies. Inbound adapters (REST controllers, message listeners) drive the application through inbound ports, and the domain reaches the outside world through outbound ports implemented by outbound adapters (database repositories, external API clients). The dependency rule is that everything points inward: the domain depends on nothing, and all infrastructure depends on the domain's interfaces, achieved through dependency inversion. It is a code-organization style that lives inside a single deployable unit, so you apply it within a monolith or within each microservice rather than instead of them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the loan-approval department at National Bank of India as the heart of the business — the rules for approving a loan never change based on how the application arrived or where records are stored. Around this heart are standardized slots (ports): one slot accepts applications, whether they come by web form, mobile app, or phone. Another slot sends records out, whether to an Oracle database or a flat file. The web form, the mobile app, the Oracle connector, and the file writer are all adapters that plug into these slots. If the bank switches from Oracle to PostgreSQL, you unplug the Oracle adapter and plug in a PostgreSQL adapter — the loan rules in the heart are not touched. The business logic does not know or care what is plugged into its slots.

**One line to remember:** Put the business rules in the center with technology-agnostic ports, plug concrete adapters onto those ports, and make everything depend inward so you can swap any technology without touching the domain.

sections.s2_technical:
The central idea is the dependency rule: dependencies always point inward, toward the domain. The domain — entities, value objects, and domain services holding the business rules — depends on nothing external. It does not import Spring, JPA, Kafka, or HTTP classes. This keeps the most valuable and most stable part of the system free of infrastructure concerns.

Ports are interfaces owned by the domain. There are two kinds. Inbound ports (also called driving ports) describe use cases the application offers, for example an interface `ApproveLoanUseCase` with a method `approve(LoanApplication)`. Outbound ports (also called driven ports) describe what the domain needs from the outside, for example `LoanRepository` with `save(Loan)` or `CreditBureauPort` with `fetchScore(customerId)`. Crucially, the domain defines these interfaces; it does not implement the outbound ones.

Adapters are the concrete implementations on the outside. Inbound adapters drive the application: a REST controller is an inbound adapter that receives an HTTP request and calls the inbound port. A Kafka listener is another inbound adapter. Outbound adapters are called by the domain through outbound ports: a JPA repository implementing `LoanRepository`, or an HTTP client implementing `CreditBureauPort`.

Dependency inversion is the mechanism that makes this work. Normally the business logic would depend on the database code. Here we invert it: the domain declares the `LoanRepository` interface, and the JPA adapter depends on and implements that interface. The high-level policy (domain) does not depend on the low-level detail (database); both depend on the abstraction, which the domain owns. At runtime, dependency injection wires the concrete adapter into the domain service through its constructor, for example `new LoanService(jpaLoanRepository, httpCreditBureau)`.

A small usage example: the domain service holds `private final LoanRepository repo;` and calls `repo.save(loan)` without knowing whether repo is backed by JPA, MongoDB, or an in-memory map. In a unit test you pass an in-memory fake implementing `LoanRepository`, so you test the business rules with zero database, zero Spring, and millisecond speed.

Why is it a style layered on top of microservices or a monolith, not an alternative? Microservices and monolith are deployment and distribution choices — how many deployable units you have and how they communicate. Hexagonal is about how you organize code inside one unit. A single microservice can be built hexagonally, and so can a monolith. You do not choose between microservices and hexagonal; you choose microservices as your deployment style and hexagonal as the internal structure of each service. The two operate on different axes.

The benefits are testability (test the domain with fakes, no infrastructure), technology independence (swap database, messaging, or framework by writing a new adapter), and clarity (the business rules are not tangled with framework annotations). A senior nuance is that strict hexagonal can feel heavy for trivial CRUD services, so the pragmatic approach is to apply it where the domain logic is rich and valuable — loan approval, settlement, fraud scoring — and keep thin CRUD services simpler. Another nuance is that the ports belong to the domain package, which is what enforces the inward dependency direction at compile time; if your domain imports your JPA entity, you have broken the architecture.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a loan-approval service whose business rules are valuable and stable, but the surrounding technology keeps changing.

Problem 1 — The database swap that broke everything. The loan rules were written directly against JPA entities and a specific repository. When the bank migrated from Oracle to PostgreSQL and later wanted a read-through cache, every change rippled into the loan rules, risking the core logic. This is exactly what hexagonal prevents — the domain should not depend on the database technology.

Problem 2 — Untestable rules. To test "approve if credit score above 700 and debt-to-income below 40 percent", the team had to spin up a database and a web server, so tests were slow and flaky. This is the testability problem hexagonal solves: with ports, the domain is tested against in-memory fakes instantly.

The fix is hexagonal. The domain defines an inbound port `ApproveLoanUseCase` and outbound ports `LoanRepository` and `CreditBureauPort`. A REST controller is the inbound adapter. An in-memory repository and a stub credit bureau are outbound adapters for the demo; in production they would be JPA and HTTP adapters.

The code will have a `Loan` domain entity, the `ApproveLoanUseCase` inbound port, the `LoanRepository` and `CreditBureauPort` outbound ports, a `LoanService` domain implementation of the use case depending only on the ports, in-memory adapters, and a demo wiring adapters into the domain and approving a loan — then swapping the credit bureau adapter without touching the domain.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: loan LN-1 for Rajesh (SAV2001), 500,000 rupees, credit score 760; then LN-2 for Priya (CUR3001), 300,000 rupees, score 620.

Step 1 — The request hits the LoanController, which is an inbound adapter. It deserializes the request and calls the inbound port ApproveLoanUseCase. The controller knows HTTP; the domain does not.

Step 2 — LoanService (the domain) creates a Loan in PENDING status. It calls the CreditBureauPort to fetch the score. The domain does not know whether the score came from an HTTP call or a stub — it only knows the port.

Step 3 — The business rule runs entirely inside the domain: score 760 is at least 700, so LN-1 becomes APPROVED. No framework code touched this decision.

Step 4 — The domain calls LoanRepository.save through the outbound port. The in-memory adapter stores it. In production a JPA adapter would persist to PostgreSQL, but the domain is unchanged.

Step 5 — For LN-2 we swap the credit-bureau adapter to one returning 620. The domain code is identical; only the plugged-in adapter changed. The rule rejects LN-2 because 620 is below 700. This demonstrates swapping infrastructure without touching the domain.

```
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Loan LN-1 for SAV2001 score=760 → APPROVED
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] --- swap credit bureau adapter (score now 620) ---
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Loan LN-2 for CUR3001 score=620 → REJECTED
```

                  InMemoryLoanRepository          StubCreditBureau

  [PENDING]──score>=700──→[APPROVED]
      │

  1. LoanController.handleApply(LN-1, SAV2001, 500000)   [inbound adapter]
  2.   → ApproveLoanUseCase.approve(...)                  [inbound port]

sections.s6_takeaway:
Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, puts the business rules at the center and surrounds them with ports, which are interfaces, and adapters, which are the concrete technology implementations that plug into those ports. The guiding rule is that all dependencies point inward: the domain depends on nothing external, it does not import Spring, JPA, or HTTP classes, and all the infrastructure depends on interfaces that the domain owns. That inward direction is achieved through dependency inversion.

There are two kinds of ports. Inbound ports describe the use cases the application offers, and inbound adapters like a REST controller or a Kafka listener drive the domain through them. Outbound ports describe what the domain needs, like a loan repository or a credit bureau client, and outbound adapters implement them against real technology. The crucial detail is that the domain declares these interfaces and the adapters implement them, so the business logic depends on an abstraction it controls rather than on a database or a framework.

In my loan service the domain held the rule that a loan is approved if the credit score is at least seven hundred. That rule lived in a plain domain service depending only on a credit bureau port and a loan repository port. I could unit test it instantly with in-memory fakes, no database and no web server, and when the bank migrated its database or swapped its credit bureau provider I only wrote a new adapter while the approval rule stayed untouched. That is the payoff: testability and technology independence.

The point I always stress is that hexagonal is not an alternative to microservices or a monolith. Microservices and monolith are about deployment and distribution, how many units you ship and how they talk, whereas hexagonal is about how you organize code inside one unit. A single microservice can be built hexagonally, and so can a monolith, so you choose microservices as your deployment style and hexagonal as the internal structure of each service; they sit on different axes and are used together. Pragmatically I apply it where the domain logic is rich and valuable, like loan approval or settlement, and keep trivial CRUD services simpler.

The one-line summary I give is: put the business rules in the center with technology-agnostic ports, plug concrete adapters onto those ports with dependencies pointing inward, and you can swap any database, messaging system, or framework by writing a new adapter without ever touching the domain.
